tierWindow.goal: Articulate criticality in your own writing: synthesise interpretations into an argument of your own, form and justify reasoned judgements, and express them in the language of criticality and your discipline's own vocabulary.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Synthesis, evaluation and construction (synthesise, judge, justify, articulate, critique); the student produces critical writing rather than recognising criticality in others.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Open, multi-source tasks: weighing several interpretations at once, defending a judgement, and controlling the precision of critical language.
tierWindow.autonomy: Low scaffolding; the learner leads, examples model expert practice, feedback refines rather than confirms; the demand is self-directed critical authorship.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner already treats being critical as a mindset and can engage with sources actively, analyse and evaluate interpretations, and recognise the basic language of criticality (the introductory and intermediate tiers). Advanced builds from reading critically to writing critically: producing a synthesised argument, a justified judgement, and precise critical language of the learner's own.

subThemes.label: Synthesis: drawing several interpretations or sources together into the formation and expression of an argument of your own
Opening up the discourse as a contributor, positioning your own argument within it
Forming judgements: the two-part form of a reasoned judgement of relative value, with its reasons
Justifying a judgement: weighing relative value and making the grounds explicit
The connective language of criticality that signals critical moves in writing
Discipline-specific vocabulary: words that carry critical meaning within your field's discourse

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, synthesising sources into an argument of your own. Second, forming and justifying judgements. Third, articulating criticality in the language and vocabulary of your discipline. Each lesson builds on the one before, moving from argument to judgement to the words that carry them.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about articulating criticality: turning critical reading into critical writing. By the end you will be able to synthesise several sources into an argument of your own, form a reasoned judgement and justify it, and articulate that judgement in the language of criticality and your discipline's own vocabulary.

These are the moves that mark advanced academic work. At this level 'be more critical' is no longer a note in the margin. The expectation is that you produce criticality on the page, building arguments, reaching judgements and defending them in writing a reader in your field will recognise.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: synthesise sources into an argument, form and justify a judgement, articulate criticality in disciplinary language.

practiceConnection.academic: Articulating criticality is what advanced academic work rewards. Every essay that asks you to construct an argument, every dissertation that weighs competing evidence, every piece of writing judged on the quality of its reasoning draws on these moves. The same capability, to synthesise, judge and justify in writing, is what research and professional practice ask of you beyond your degree.

decidedValue.whereNextOmitted: Advanced is the top tier of the criticality pathway; resolve-agent-author omits the where-next slot at advanced, so no where-next block is authored. Horizontal links are noted for metadata only.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Articulating criticality is now something you can do on the page. You can synthesise several sources into an argument of your own, rather than summarising each in turn. You can form a reasoned judgement of relative value and justify it with the evidence it rests on. And you can articulate that judgement in the language of criticality and your discipline's own vocabulary, so the reasoning is visible in the writing. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, articulating criticality is something you practise in every piece of advanced work. Each argument you construct from several sources, each judgement you reach and defend, each term you choose for its precise meaning is this capability at work. It is also what research and professional life reward: the ability to weigh evidence and argue a position, in writing, with reasons.
